title: Public Goods
description: Non-rival, non-excludable goods — free riders, Samuelson condition

concepts.title: Two Defining Properties
concepts.contentHtml:
A public good has two unusual properties.

Non-rivalry: one person's consumption doesn't reduce what's available to others. A streetlight illuminates the whole street; my looking at it doesn't dim it for you.

Non-excludability: you can't easily prevent non-payers from benefiting. National defense protects every citizen whether they paid taxes or not.

Goods that are both: pure public goods. National defense, basic research, clean air, lighthouses (the textbook example), GPS signals.

Many real goods are partially public. Toll roads are non-rival (until congested) but excludable. Public TV broadcasts are non-excludable but congestion isn't an issue. Each property creates different problems.

concepts.title: The Free Rider Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Why do markets under-provide public goods?

Because of free riders. If a good is non-excludable, rational individuals can wait for someone else to pay. If everyone reasons this way, no one pays, and the good doesn't get produced — even when its total value far exceeds its cost.

Classic example: voluntary national defense. If donations were optional, most people would free-ride on others' contributions. Defense would be drastically underfunded.

The market failure isn't a glitch — it's structural. Voluntary provision can't aggregate willingness-to-pay when individuals can benefit without paying.

Solutions involve forcing contribution: taxes for government provision; mandatory association dues; tying public goods to private goods (advertising-funded broadcasting); social pressure in small communities.

concepts.title: The Samuelson Condition
concepts.contentHtml:
Paul Samuelson (1954) derived the optimal level of public good provision.

For a private good: provide where each person's marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost.

For a public good: provide where the sum of all individuals' marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost. Σ MRS = MC.

Why the sum? Because the same unit of public good is consumed by everyone simultaneously (non-rivalry). The total benefit is the aggregate.

This implies more provision is generally optimal than individual willingness-to-pay would suggest. It also implies that knowing how much to provide requires knowing everyone's preferences — which they have an incentive to misrepresent (claim low to free-ride, claim high if costs are shared).

The result: aggregating preferences for public goods is a fundamentally hard mechanism-design problem. Voting, surveys, and revealed-preference inference all have flaws.

concepts.title: Club Goods and Common-Pool Resources
concepts.contentHtml:
Goods that are partially public take two main forms.

Club goods: non-rival but excludable. Cable TV, gym membership, software. The provider can charge for access, and additional users don't dilute existing users' benefits (much). Markets can provide these reasonably well.

Common-pool resources (CPRs): rival but non-excludable. Fisheries, atmospheric carbon sink, groundwater, public roads (when congested). Use by one reduces availability for others, but exclusion is costly.

CPRs face the tragedy of the commons: each user has incentive to use more than the socially optimal amount, since they bear only their share of the depletion cost. Fisheries collapse, aquifers drain, traffic jams.

Elinor Ostrom's Nobel-winning research showed that communities often successfully self-govern CPRs through informal rules — challenging the simple state-vs-market framing of public goods debates.

concepts.title: Provision in Practice
concepts.contentHtml:
How do societies actually provide public goods?

Government provision financed by taxes. Most pure public goods (defense, courts, basic research) are funded this way.

Private provision with public benefit. Open-source software, much basic science, philanthropic foundations. Free riding exists but doesn't fully prevent provision.

Tying to private goods. Advertising funds broadcasting; cellular networks fund GPS apps that bundle public-domain location services.

Mandatory associations. Property owners' associations charge dues; some industries levy mandatory contributions to research consortiums.

International coordination. Global public goods (climate stability, pandemic preparedness) face severe free-rider problems across countries with no overarching authority. Treaties, side-payments, and reputation are partial substitutes.

The pattern: pure markets under-provide; pure government provision creates inefficiency in other ways; the practical solutions are usually hybrid and imperfect.

title: Externalities & Pigouvian Taxes
description: Internalizing social costs — Coase theorem and its limits

concepts.title: When Private Costs Diverge from Social
concepts.contentHtml:
Markets work when the people making decisions face the full costs and benefits. Externalities arise when they don't.

A factory pollutes — the pollution harms downstream residents. The factory's private cost is below the social cost (which includes the residents' damages). The factory produces too much.

A vaccinated person reduces disease transmission to others. Their private benefit is below the social benefit. Vaccination is under-provided.

The wedge between private and social calculus is the source of inefficiency. Welfare economics is largely about diagnosing these wedges and proposing corrections.
mathExpressions: MSC = MPC + MEC, \quad MSB = MPB + MEB

concepts.title: Pigouvian Taxes and Subsidies
concepts.contentHtml:
Arthur Pigou's 1920 prescription: tax negative externalities, subsidize positive ones — at a rate equal to the marginal external effect.

A Pigouvian tax raises the polluter's private cost to match the social cost. They internalize what they used to externalize. Output falls to the social optimum.

A Pigouvian subsidy works the other way: research subsidies, vaccination subsidies, education subsidies for activities with positive spillovers.

The key insight: prices that reflect full social costs are the simplest fix. The tax gives polluters flexibility — they can reduce emissions or pay the tax, whichever is cheaper. This produces efficient abatement, with reductions concentrated where they're cheapest.
mathExpressions: t^* = MEC \text{ at the social optimum}

concepts.title: The Coase Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Ronald Coase's 1960 challenge: under specific conditions, externalities don't require government intervention. Private bargaining can fix them.

The Coase theorem: if property rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are zero, parties will negotiate to the efficient outcome regardless of who initially holds the rights.

Example: factory emits smoke; residents are harmed. If residents have a right to clean air, the factory must pay them to pollute. If the factory has a right to pollute, residents must pay them to stop. Either way, bargaining gets to the same efficient pollution level. Only the distribution of welfare differs.

The key qualifier: under those conditions. Real transaction costs are large. Bargaining among many parties is hard. Information is asymmetric. Coase's point wasn't that externalities are non-problems — it was that we should ask why bargaining can't fix them in each case.

concepts.title: Carbon Pricing
concepts.contentHtml:
The biggest contemporary application of Pigouvian thinking: carbon emissions.

Climate change is a vast negative externality — emissions impose costs on everyone, especially future generations.

Two main approaches:

Carbon tax: set a price per ton of CO₂. Sweden's, introduced in 1991 at a modest rate, now exceeds $100/ton; Switzerland, Norway and others have meaningful carbon taxes (British Columbia scrapped its well-known consumer carbon tax in 2025).

Cap-and-trade: set a quantity cap, issue permits, let them trade. EU ETS covers ~40% of EU emissions. California's program covers most of its emissions.

Both are Pigouvian in spirit. The tax sets the price and lets quantities adjust; cap-and-trade sets the quantity and lets price adjust.

Most economists prefer either to direct regulation, which lacks the flexibility of letting markets find the cheapest abatement. The political economy is harder — direct subsidies for clean tech (Inflation Reduction Act in the US) are easier to pass than visible taxes.

concepts.title: Limits and Practicalities
concepts.contentHtml:
The textbook story is cleaner than reality.

Setting the right price. The marginal external cost is hard to estimate. Climate damages depend on uncertain future outcomes. The 'social cost of carbon' has been estimated from $50 to $400+ per ton depending on assumptions about discount rates, climate sensitivity, and damage functions.

Multiple externalities. Cars produce CO₂, local air pollution, congestion, accident risk. A single tax can't optimally address all four. Bundles of instruments (gasoline taxes plus congestion pricing plus liability rules) come closer.

Distributional effects. Pigouvian taxes are typically regressive in incidence — poorer households spend higher shares on energy and travel. Revenue recycling (carbon dividends) can offset this.

Political economy. Visible taxes face political resistance even when efficient. Australia's carbon tax was repealed two years after enactment. France's gasoline tax sparked the gilets jaunes protests.

The Pigouvian framework remains the right starting point. The implementation challenges shape what's actually possible.

title: Taxation & Deadweight Loss
description: Tax incidence, elasticity rules, Ramsey rule, optimal income taxation

concepts.title: What Taxes Do to Markets
concepts.contentHtml:
A tax drives a wedge between the price the buyer pays and the price the seller receives. Both quantities and prices change.

Standard analysis: with the tax, the price buyers pay rises; the price sellers receive falls; quantity transacted falls. The government collects revenue (tax × quantity).

The deadweight loss (DWL) is the economic value of trades that no longer happen — would-be buyers willing to pay more than would-be sellers' costs, but blocked by the tax wedge. Visual: the triangle between the demand and supply curves bounded by the new equilibrium.

DWL is a pure efficiency loss. Buyers lose, sellers lose, government revenue offsets only some of the loss. The remainder is genuinely destroyed value.

concepts.title: Tax Incidence
concepts.contentHtml:
Tax incidence — who actually pays — depends on elasticities, not on who's legally responsible for remitting the tax.

The general rule: the side of the market that's more inelastic bears more of the burden.

Cigarette taxes fall mostly on smokers, because cigarette demand is inelastic. Land taxes fall entirely on landowners — land supply is perfectly inelastic.

Payroll taxes are nominally split between employer and employee, but most evidence suggests workers bear most of the incidence (labor supply is more inelastic than labor demand in most settings).

The legal-economic distinction matters because policy debates often confuse them. A tax 'on corporations' may largely fall on consumers (through higher prices), workers (through lower wages), or shareholders (through lower returns), depending on elasticities.

concepts.title: DWL Grows with the Square of the Tax Rate
concepts.contentHtml:
A useful approximation: deadweight loss is roughly proportional to (tax rate)² × elasticity.

Implication: doubling a tax rate quadruples the DWL.

Practical consequence: many small taxes are more efficient than a few big ones (the Ramsey rule). Broad-based, low-rate taxes hurt less than narrow, high-rate ones.

Also: the more elastic the affected market, the more painful the tax. Taxing things people respond to strongly (luxury goods, mobile capital, easily-substituted activities) creates more DWL than taxing things they can't easily avoid (necessities, immobile factors, addictions).

This is one reason most economists prefer broad consumption taxes (VAT, sales taxes) and land taxes over high-rate income or capital taxes.

concepts.title: Ramsey Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
Frank Ramsey (1927) — yes, the same Ramsey as the math one — solved for the structure of taxes that minimizes total DWL given a revenue requirement.

The Ramsey rule: tax goods inversely to their elasticity. Inelastic goods bear higher tax rates; elastic goods bear lower rates.

Why? Because elastic goods produce more behavioral distortion (more DWL) per dollar raised. Inelastic goods are 'fixed' targets that yield revenue without much behavioral change.

Real-world echoes: taxes on cigarettes, alcohol, gasoline (all inelastic), even setting aside externality justifications. Property taxes (land is inelastic in supply). Sin taxes more broadly.

Ramsey's rule clashes with equity considerations. Inelastic goods often include necessities, which the poor consume in larger income shares. Pure efficiency would tax bread and medicine; equity says don't.

The compromise: optimal tax theory blends Ramsey efficiency with redistribution motives.

concepts.title: Optimal Income Taxation
concepts.contentHtml:
James Mirrlees's 1971 framework (Nobel 1996): how should income taxes be structured?

Tradeoff: high marginal rates on the rich raise revenue and redistribute, but discourage labor supply and effort. Low rates preserve incentives but limit redistribution.

Mirrlees's result: optimal marginal rates depend on three things — the elasticity of taxable income (how much people change behavior), the inequality of skills (how concentrated income is at the top), and the social weight on redistribution.

Key empirical implications:

– U-shaped optimal rates: higher at the bottom (where work-vs-welfare tradeoffs matter), lower in the middle, higher at the top (where rates can be high without large efficiency costs if elasticities are low).

– Top rates around 50-70% are within the plausible range, depending on elasticity assumptions.

– Negative income taxes / EITC structures are often near-optimal for low incomes — encouraging work while supporting low earners.

The framework remains the workhorse of tax policy analysis, with continuous refinements from Diamond-Saez and others.

title: Social Welfare
description: Pareto efficiency, social welfare functions, Arrow's impossibility

concepts.title: Pareto Efficiency
concepts.contentHtml:
An allocation is Pareto efficient if no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.

Pareto efficiency is a minimal welfare criterion. It says nothing about distribution — an allocation where one person has everything and others have nothing is Pareto efficient (you can't help others without taking from the one).

Pareto improvements (changes that help someone without hurting anyone) are uncontroversial — by definition no one objects. Pareto-noncomparable changes (where some win and some lose) require some other criterion to evaluate.

The First Welfare Theorem: under perfect competition, no externalities, and complete information, equilibrium allocations are Pareto efficient. The Invisible Hand result.

The Second Welfare Theorem: any Pareto-efficient allocation can be achieved through markets if initial wealth is appropriately redistributed. Equity and efficiency are separable in principle.

concepts.title: Social Welfare Functions
concepts.contentHtml:
To rank allocations beyond Pareto, you need a social welfare function (SWF) that aggregates individual utilities.

Common forms:

Utilitarian: W = Σu_i. Sum of utilities. Equal weight on each person. Maximizes total welfare regardless of distribution.

Rawlsian: W = min(u_i). Society is only as well off as its worst-off member. Maximin justice.

Generalized utilitarian: W = Σ f(u_i). With concave f, weighted toward those with low utility — equity-weighted utilitarianism.

Bentham 'each to count for one and none for more than one': the original utilitarian intuition — democratic and impartial.

Each SWF embeds a particular ethical view. Choice of SWF substitutes one set of value judgments (about distribution) for another (about who counts).

concepts.title: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Kenneth Arrow's 1951 theorem (Nobel 1972) is one of the deepest results in social choice theory.

Arrow asked: is there a method of aggregating individual preferences into social preferences that satisfies a few minimal conditions?

The conditions:

– Unrestricted domain: the rule must work for any individual preferences.

– Pareto: if everyone prefers A to B, society does too.

– Independence of irrelevant alternatives: social ranking of A vs B depends only on individual rankings of A vs B.

– Non-dictatorship: no single individual decides.

– Transitivity: social preferences are well-ordered.

Arrow's Theorem: no rule can satisfy all five simultaneously, unless there are only two alternatives.

This is striking. Democratic preference aggregation, on minimal axiomatic foundations, is provably impossible.

concepts.title: Implications of Arrow
concepts.contentHtml:
Arrow's result shapes our understanding of voting and social choice.

Different voting rules violate different axioms. Plurality voting can produce 'spoiler' candidates and Condorcet violations. Borda count violates IIA. Approval voting, ranked-choice, and other systems each have characteristic failures.

No system is uniformly better than others — they trade off Arrow's axioms differently. The question 'what's the best voting rule?' depends on which violations matter most in context.

The deeper lesson: democratic preference aggregation isn't a value-free 'will of the people.' Different aggregation rules produce different outcomes from the same individual preferences. The method of aggregation is itself a normative choice.

Sen's response: relax Arrow's stringent axioms (especially IIA) and we get usable aggregation rules with reasonable properties. Pragmatic social choice can work, even if perfect aggregation can't.

concepts.title: Inequality Measurement
concepts.contentHtml:
To evaluate redistribution, you need measures of inequality.

The Gini coefficient is the most common single number — 0 means perfect equality, 1 means one person has everything. Most developed countries have Ginis between about 0.25 (Nordic) and about 0.40 (US, after taxes and transfers). Brazil and South Africa exceed 0.50 — among the world's most unequal.

The Lorenz curve plots cumulative income share against cumulative population share. Perfect equality is the diagonal. Inequality bows the curve below the diagonal. Gini is twice the area between the diagonal and the curve.

Other measures include: 90/10 ratio, top-share statistics (income share of top 1%, top 10%), Atkinson indices (parameterized by inequality aversion), Theil index.

Each measure captures different facets. Gini is averaged across the distribution; top shares emphasize the right tail; 90/10 ratios emphasize the bottom-to-middle gap. Looking at one measure alone misses important variation.

The 21st century has seen rising top-end inequality in most developed countries (Piketty, Saez, Atkinson) — the top 1% share has roughly doubled in the US since 1980. Gini coefficients have moved less dramatically, since they're less sensitive to top-end shifts. Choice of measure affects what story the data tells.

title: Healthcare Economics
description: Adverse selection, moral hazard, single payer vs insurance markets

concepts.title: Why Healthcare Is Different
concepts.contentHtml:
Healthcare is one of the largest sectors in advanced economies (~10-18% of GDP) and one of the worst-functioning by standard market metrics.

Distinctive features that break ordinary supply-demand analysis:

– Asymmetric information: patients can't easily evaluate medical advice; providers know much more.

– Insurance: someone else (insurer or government) pays at the point of care, distorting demand.

– High and unpredictable costs: a serious illness can cost more than lifetime income.

– Externalities: infectious disease control benefits everyone.

– Moral concerns: denying lifesaving treatment for inability to pay strikes most societies as unacceptable.

– Market power: hospitals, drug patent holders, and specialist providers often have monopoly-style pricing power.

These features mean pure-market healthcare doesn't deliver the efficient outcomes the textbook predicts.

concepts.title: Adverse Selection in Insurance
concepts.contentHtml:
Insurance markets face a fundamental information problem: insurers can't perfectly observe risk. Sicker people benefit more from insurance than healthier people.

The result: adverse selection. At any premium price, sicker people sign up disproportionately. Average claims exceed predictions; insurers raise premiums; healthier people drop out; the pool gets sicker still. The market unravels.

Akerlof's lemons logic applied to insurance.

Solutions:

– Risk-rating (charge higher premiums for higher-risk individuals). Efficient but punishes the sick — politically and ethically problematic.

– Mandate enrollment (force everyone in, mixing risks). The Affordable Care Act's individual mandate worked this way.

– Single payer (everyone covered by default; risk pooling is automatic).

– Employer-based pooling (group enrollment averages risks). Most US private insurance.

– Subsidies for high-risk pools.

Every advanced country has some mechanism to overcome adverse selection. Pure private insurance markets without these mechanisms don't function.

concepts.title: Moral Hazard
concepts.contentHtml:
Once insured, you face only a small fraction of the cost of additional care. Moral hazard: insured people use more healthcare than they would otherwise.

Some moral hazard is desirable — encouraging preventive care, reducing financial barriers to needed treatment. Some isn't — emergency-room visits for minor problems, demand for expensive treatments with limited benefit.

Cost-sharing tools (deductibles, copays, coinsurance) push back against moral hazard. The RAND Health Insurance Experiment (1970s) randomly assigned people to different cost-sharing levels. Result: higher cost-sharing reduced healthcare use ~30% with minimal effect on health outcomes for most people — but worse outcomes for the chronically ill and lower-income.

The implication: cost-sharing efficiently constrains moderate use but harms vulnerable populations. Modern designs try to target high-value services (preventive care, chronic disease management) with low cost-sharing while imposing higher cost-sharing on low-value services.

concepts.title: International Comparisons
concepts.contentHtml:
Different countries have very different healthcare systems and outcomes.

Single-payer (UK NHS, Canada, Taiwan): government insurance, often government provision. Universal coverage; lower per-capita costs; sometimes longer waits; usually good outcomes by international standards.

Multi-payer with universal coverage (Germany, France, Netherlands, Switzerland): regulated insurance markets with mandates. Universal coverage; intermediate costs; generally good outcomes.

Mixed (US): employer-based for ~50%, public (Medicare, Medicaid) for ~35%, marketplace plans for ~7%, uninsured for ~8%. Highest per-capita costs in the world (~$13,000 vs ~$6,000 OECD average), middling outcomes, persistent uninsurance.

The US pays roughly twice the OECD average per capita for outcomes that aren't proportionately better. Drivers include higher prices (drugs, devices, salaries), administrative complexity, end-of-life intensity, and the absence of strong cost-control mechanisms.

No system is universally best. The single-payer countries trade some choice and immediacy for cost control. The multi-payer countries trade some redistribution for choice. The US trades cost control and universal coverage for clinical innovation and consumer choice.

concepts.title: Cost Growth and Reform
concepts.contentHtml:
Healthcare cost growth is the central fiscal challenge for most advanced countries.

Drivers: aging populations, expensive new technologies, rising chronic disease, end-of-life intensity, market power of providers, and Baumol's cost disease (services with limited productivity growth become relatively expensive over time).

Cost-control approaches:

– Price negotiation (single-payer power, formulary pressure).

– Bundled payments (paying for episodes rather than services).

– Capitation (paying providers a fixed amount per patient).

– Health technology assessment (UK's NICE, Germany's IQWIG): evaluating whether new treatments are worth their costs before approving public payment.

– Care coordination for high-cost patients.

– Prevention: reducing demand for expensive care through public health.

Most reforms work modestly. None has solved the long-run cost growth problem. Healthcare's combination of inelastic demand for life-saving care, accelerating technology, and aging populations makes it a uniquely difficult sector for cost control.

title: Education Economics
description: Returns to schooling, vouchers, peer effects, the credentialing debate

concepts.title: Returns to Schooling
concepts.contentHtml:
Cross-country and cross-individual evidence consistently shows education raises lifetime earnings substantially.

Mincer estimates: ~6-10% earnings boost per year of schooling. IV estimates from compulsory-schooling-law shifts often confirm the magnitude.

Returns are higher in some settings: STEM fields, professional degrees, technical training. Lower in others: some humanities, low-quality institutions.

The aggregate implications: education raises GDP per capita through the human capital channel. The Solow-Romer literature attributes substantial growth differences across countries to education differences.

For individuals, education usually has positive expected NPV — even at high US tuition costs, four-year degrees in employable fields earn back their costs many times over. The exceptions: low-completion programs at expensive institutions, fields with weak labor markets, students who'd have done well in trades.

concepts.title: Public Provision and Externalities
concepts.contentHtml:
Why is education publicly provided in most countries?

Several reasons.

Positive externalities: educated populations support democratic institutions, productive workforces, scientific progress. Private decisions under-invest because individuals capture only part of the social benefit.

Credit constraints: students from poor families can't easily borrow against future earnings to fund education. Public provision relaxes this.

Information failures: 18-year-olds may not appreciate education's long-term value.

Equity: education is a major channel of intergenerational mobility. Public provision aims to give children equal opportunity regardless of family background.

The mechanisms are debated. Direct public provision (typical for K-12), public funding with private provision (vouchers, charter schools), and government-subsidized private institutions (US college aid) all produce education with public-good characteristics. Each has efficiency-equity tradeoffs.

concepts.title: Vouchers and School Choice
concepts.contentHtml:
The case for school choice: market discipline improves quality. Parents choose; schools compete; better schools expand and worse ones contract.

Vouchers give parents public money to spend at public or private schools. Charter schools are publicly funded but operate with more autonomy than traditional public schools. Magnet schools offer specialized programs to attract motivated students.

Empirical evidence is mixed. Some voucher programs show small positive effects (Milwaukee, DC, Florida); some show no effects or negative effects (Indiana, Louisiana). Charter schools vary enormously — top-performing 'no excuses' charters (KIPP, Success Academy, Harlem Children's Zone) show large gains; the average effect across all charters is closer to neutral.

Tradeoffs: choice systems may improve average outcomes but increase sorting, with motivated families clustering in better schools and concentrated disadvantage in others. The debate isn't 'choice vs no-choice' but how to design choice systems that improve quality without exacerbating inequality.

concepts.title: Peer Effects
concepts.contentHtml:
Students learn not just from teachers but from each other. Peer effects are an important — and often understudied — input to educational outcomes.

Identification challenges: peers are endogenous — students sort into classrooms with similar backgrounds. Random assignment is rare.

Studies that exploit random variation (military academies, dorm assignments, student rotation policies) generally find significant peer effects, though magnitudes vary. Stronger peers tend to lift weaker students; the reverse is also true but smaller.

Implications for school design: tracking (separating students by ability) can help advanced students by concentrating them but hurt struggling students by removing peer role models. The optimal design depends on the specific mix.

Peer effects also matter outside the classroom: social networks shape college majors, career choices, even risk preferences. Career-track sorting is partly social, not just individual.

concepts.title: The Credentialing Debate
concepts.contentHtml:
How much of education's value is human capital (skills) vs signaling (credentials)?

Evidence for human capital: schooling improves measurable cognitive skills, especially in literacy and numeracy. Specific training (medicine, engineering) clearly delivers job-specific skills. Health and parenting outcomes improve with education.

Evidence for signaling: 'sheepskin effects' — wage jumps associated with degree completion, not gradual schooling. Differences across majors much larger than differences from random extra months of schooling. Employers screen by university brand, sometimes ignoring content.

Most educational economics rejects the pure signaling view (Caplan) but acknowledges signaling is real. Both effects coexist; the proportions vary by field and level.

Policy implications: if education is largely signaling, public subsidies are wasteful (we're paying for people to acquire credentials that don't add productivity). If largely human capital, subsidies fix market failures and produce broad gains. Most reforms (alternative credentialing, apprenticeships, competency-based learning) try to provide skill verification without traditional academic length.

The 2020s have seen experiments: Google certificates, IBM apprenticeships, coding bootcamps. Whether they substitute for traditional degrees in the labor market remains an open question.
